questions.prompt: Why does std::expected<T, E> provide the wrapper type std::unexpected<E>?
options: Because E is always heap-allocated separately from T
To disambiguate error construction when T and E have the same or convertible types
Because E cannot be a scoped enum without wrapping
To automatically convert error return values into thrown exceptions
questions.explanation: If you return a plain value from a function returning std::expected<int, int> or std::expected<std::string, std::string_view>, overload resolution cannot tell whether an argument is a value or an error. std::unexpected(e) unambiguously selects the error alternative.

questions.prompt: In <system_error>, what is the primary design difference between std::error_code and std::error_condition?
options: error_code represents platform/domain-specific raw codes, while error_condition represents portable semantic categories for matching
error_condition throws exceptions automatically whereas error_code does not
error_code allocates a std::string message while error_condition holds only an int
error_code is only for Windows APIs and error_condition is only for POSIX errno
questions.explanation: std::error_code preserves the exact platform or library error integer and category pointer, whereas std::error_condition (like std::errc) represents a portable abstraction you compare against via category equivalence.

questions.prompt: What does the following C++23 code evaluate?
options: Branch B runs because the contained bool is false
Compilation fails because optional<bool> has an ambiguous operator bool
Branch A runs because explicit operator bool() checks engagement, not the wrapped bool
Undefined behavior because optional<bool> cannot hold false
questions.explanation: std::optional<T>::operator bool() always returns has_value(). Because flag holds the value false, it is engaged, so if (flag) enters Branch A. Use flag == true or flag.value_or(false) to test the contained value.

questions.prompt: Given std::expected<int, std::string> r = 42;, what happens if you immediately call r.error() without checking r.has_value()?
questions.code:
std::expected<int, std::string> r = 42;
auto& msg = r.error();
options: It returns an empty default-constructed std::string
It throws std::bad_expected_access<int>
Compilation fails unless wrapped in a try block
It triggers undefined behavior because r holds a value, not an error
questions.explanation: Unlike r.value(), which throws std::bad_expected_access when holding an error, r.error() is an unchecked observer whose precondition is !has_value(). Calling r.error() on a value-holding expected is undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: When registering a custom enum class AppErr with std::error_code via std::is_error_code_enum<AppErr>, where must make_error_code(AppErr) be declared?
options: Inside namespace std alongside std::is_error_code_enum
Inside the same namespace as AppErr so ADL finds it
As a static member function of std::error_category
Only inside the translation unit defining main()
questions.explanation: std::error_code's template constructor invokes unqualified make_error_code(e) so argument-dependent lookup (ADL) locates the overload in AppErr's associated namespace. Adding function overloads to namespace std is undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: In C++23, which call correctly transforms only the error channel of std::expected<int, ParseErr> e while passing any T value straight through?
options: e.or_else(map_err)
e.and_then(map_err)
e.transform_error(map_err)
e.transform(map_err)
questions.explanation: transform_error(f) applies f(*this->error()) when !has_value() and wraps the result in std::unexpected, returning a std::expected<T, NewErr>. If has_value() is true, transform_error forwards the existing T value unchanged.
